name: Krautrock
about: Krautrock is the name the British press gave to the experimental rock that came out of West Germany between roughly 1968 and 1976. Its makers shared less a sound than a refusal: of Anglo-American blues rock, of the song, of the past. Can built hypnotic, edited-down grooves around Jaki Liebezeit's drumming; Neu! stripped rock to the motorik pulse; Faust cut up tape in a Wümme farmhouse; Kraftwerk, Tangerine Dream and Klaus Schulze moved toward synthesizers; Popol Vuh and Amon Düül II drifted toward the sacred and the communal. Producer Conny Plank sat behind much of it. The records sold little at home but seeded post-punk, ambient, techno and post-rock, and the motorik beat is now simply part of rock's vocabulary.

artists.name: Can
artists.why: the Cologne band at the genre's centre

artists.name: Kraftwerk
artists.why: from Düsseldorf jams to electronic pop

artists.name: Harmonia
artists.why: Cluster plus Rother, the Forst supergroup

artists.name: Conny Plank
artists.why: the producer behind most of it

albums.title: Tago Mago
albums.why: A double album of edited jams, with Damo Suzuki's mutter-and-howl over Liebezeit's unerring pulse; the 'Halleluhwah' groove alone justifies the genre's reputation.

albums.title: Neu!
albums.why: Rother and Dinger's debut invents the motorik beat on 'Hallogallo' and then spends the rest of the record taking it apart; endlessly influential.

albums.title: Ege Bamyasi
albums.why: The tighter, funkier follow-up, with 'Vitamin C' and 'Spoon' proving that the Can groove could fit inside a pop song without losing its strangeness.

albums.title: Faust IV
albums.why: Their most approachable record, opening with the twelve-minute drone 'Krautrock' and ranging through pastoral folk, tape collage and the deadpan 'The Sad Skinhead'.

albums.title: Yeti
albums.why: The Munich commune's sprawling double album: heavy riffs, violin, chanting and a side of improvisation that defined the genre's hairier, acid-soaked wing.

albums.title: Autobahn
albums.why: The 22-minute title track turned a drive on the motorway into minimalist electronic pop and gave Kraftwerk an unlikely American hit.

albums.title: Phaedra
albums.why: Sequencer-driven and deeply atmospheric, the record that moved the Berlin School from guitar freak-outs to the pulsing synthesizer music it is known for.

albums.title: Hosianna Mantra
albums.why: Florian Fricke abandoned the Moog for piano, oboe and Djong Yun's voice on a devotional record of rare stillness; Herzog's films would never sound the same.

albums.title: Neu! 75
albums.why: Split between a serene Rother side and a snarling Dinger side, with 'Hero' and 'After Eight' anticipating punk by a year or two.

albums.title: Faust
albums.why: Pressed on clear vinyl in a clear sleeve, the debut is three long pieces of tape splicing and collapsing rock: baffling in 1971, prophetic since.

albums.title: Deluxe
albums.why: Rother, Moebius and Roedelius with Guru Guru's Mani Neumeier on drums, nudging their pastoral electronics toward actual songs on 'Deluxe (Immer Wieder)'.

albums.title: Zuckerzeit
albums.why: Produced with Michael Rother, the duo's sweetest record: short, bubbling rhythm-box pieces that point straight at ambient techno.

albums.title: Ash Ra Tempel
albums.why: Manuel Göttsching, Hartmut Enke and Klaus Schulze stretching one riff and one drone across two sides: the Berlin space-rock blueprint.

albums.title: Phallus Dei
albums.why: The debut, raw and rambling with its side-long title piece, is the first great document of the Munich underground.

albums.title: Malesch
albums.why: A Berlin band back from a tour of Egypt and Greece, blending field recordings with liquid guitar jams; the most travelled record in the genre.

albums.title: Irrlicht
albums.why: One organ, a filtered orchestra and no rhythm at all: Schulze's solo debut is dark, slow and the root of a long career in electronic drift.

albums.title: In den Gärten Pharaos
albums.why: Fricke's big Moog and Frank Fiedler's percussion on side one, a cathedral organ on side two; the bridge between early cosmic music and ambient.

albums.title: Musik von Harmonia
albums.why: The first meeting of Cluster and Rother, a warm, slightly wobbly set of electronic instrumentals that Eno called the world's most important rock group.

albums.title: La Düsseldorf
albums.why: Klaus Dinger's post-Neu! band taking the motorik pulse somewhere brighter and more anthemic; a hit in Germany and a cult elsewhere.

albums.title: Flammende Herzen
albums.why: Rother's first solo record, with Jaki Liebezeit drumming, distils his melodic side into glowing guitar instrumentals of great calm.

albums.title: UFO
albums.why: Mani Neumeier's trio at their most unhinged, a wall of fuzz and free drumming that made the Hendrix connection explicit.

albums.title: E2-E4
albums.why: An hour of sequenced minimalism recorded in one 1981 take and released three years later; Balearic DJs and house producers adopted it.

albums.title: Beak>
albums.why: Geoff Barrow's Bristol trio reviving the Can groove with live-in-the-room recordings and nothing overdubbed; a faithful and quietly intense tribute.

albums.title: Radiate!
albums.why: A Berlin trio who began by busking motorik in subway stations, and whose Bureau B debut captures the beat with raw momentum.
